title: “Where Do We Even Start?”
deck: A quick start for parents asking for PDA support, help across classes, music inclusion or a new school music program.
sections: 1. Pick the thing that needs to change.

Does staff need to understand your child’s PDA profile? Is getting help too public? Is music missing or hard to access? Choose one starting point. You do not need to solve the whole school experience before sending an email.
2. Bring one real example.
“When they forget a worksheet, they have to ask in front of everyone. They get stuck and the lesson moves on.” That tells the team more than “They need to be more independent.”
3. Ask for something the adults can provide.
“Could there be spare copies in a known place, with someone showing them how to use it?” For music, that might be an instrument loan, an adapted part or teaching time for a new class.
4. Write down who will do what.
Agree on a first step, the adult responsible, a backup and a review date. Ask your child what changed for them. Quietly getting through the day is only part of the picture.
prompt: Could we meet to discuss [barrier] and try [support], so my child can [what they want to do]?

title: “But They Did It Yesterday.”
deck: A parent handout about PDA, autonomy and why today may need different support.
sections: Start here: what is PDA?

PDA usually means Pathological Demand Avoidance. Some people prefer Persistent Drive for Autonomy. Families use it to describe intense difficulty with demands. Researchers are still debating how to define and assess the profile.
1. Describe what happens, not just the label.
Does “come and ask me” make getting help harder? Does the same task go differently when the room is quieter? Write down the demand, the setting and what your child says about it.
2. Ask for fewer hurdles.

A shared charger, spare music or instructions on the board can remove a whole conversation. Agree on honest choices: start here or there, use this format or that one. An adult can help your child learn the routine.
3. Make room for today.
Knowing how to do something and being able to manage it right now are different things. Ask what support is available on a harder day. Yesterday is useful information. It is not an invoice due today.
prompt: They know how to [skill]. What seems to get in the way today is [barrier]. Could we try [support]?

title: “What If a Mistake Was Just Information?”
deck: Help the school teach what to do after something goes wrong, in music and in other classrooms.
quote:
A wrong note is information.
It is not a character reference.
sections: 1. Find out what happens after the mistake.
When your child loses their place, forgets music or answers incorrectly, what comes next? A correction they can use? A public reminder? Ten minutes trying not to cry? Start with their experience.
2. Ask for a route back in.

“That should be F-sharp” gives information. “You never pay attention” adds a judgement. Ask for a clear next step, a quieter cue or a resource they can reach themselves. The spare-music binder should not come with a lecture.
3. Make the same route available elsewhere.

If grabbing spare music works in band, could spare worksheets work in math? The other teacher needs to provide the resource and teach the routine, too. “You can do it in band” is not the missing support.
prompt: When [mistake] happens, could the next step be [usable help], so they can get back to learning?

title: “Can the Worry Committee Take a Break?”
deck: Explore whether music gives your child some breathing room. Let them help decide.
sections: 1. Ask what already helps.
A familiar song? A keyboard pattern? Headphones? Quiet? Singing helped reduce reported worry in one adult study, but your child gets a say in what feels useful to them.
2. Make the option easy to use.

Could there be an agreed place, time and signal for a short musical break? Sort out supervision and volume beforehand. A student should not have to explain every thought to earn a few minutes of space.
3. Check in without turning it into homework.
“More settled, the same or more stirred up?” A gesture or a later chat might be enough. They can change their mind. Yesterday’s helpful song is not a lifetime contract.
And listen to what the worry is about.
If bullying, noise or another problem keeps causing distress, adults still need to address it. A song does not fix a harmful situation. Keep other needed support available.
prompt: Could we offer [chosen option] at [time/place], with a simple way to start and stop?

title: “What Could Music Make Possible Here?”
deck: A short research companion for families advocating for school music. Start with the musical learning.
sections: 1. Name what students are missing.
A chance to play, compose, listen, perform or make music with other people. Those are worthwhile things to learn. Your child does not need a higher math mark to justify the instrument.
2. Choose research that fits the conversation.

Habibi and colleagues follow auditory learning and related brain changes. Jamey and colleagues examine inhibitory control: holding back an automatic response. Sala and Gobet examine broader academic claims. These are different questions, so choose the source that fits your request.
3. Connect it to an actual school opportunity.

Are you asking for inclusion in an existing class, an instrument loan, a beginner ensemble or a new program? Name the teaching and support needed. “Music is good for kids” is a starting point. A usable class needs time, resources and someone to teach it.
What about music therapy?

Music-therapy studies involve a different professional service. If you are asking for music education, focus on learning music, participation and access. You can discuss therapy separately when that is what your child needs.
prompt: We would like students to have access to [musical learning]. Could we discuss [teaching, resources and support] to make that possible?

title: “Everyone Welcome. But Can Everyone Get In?”
deck: Turn an invitation to music into something your child can actually use.
sections: 1. Find the barrier at the door.

Is it the fee, instrument, noise, transport, audition or instructions? Does your child have to be calm and organised before they can enter the class that might help them feel connected? Ask them what makes joining difficult.
2. Ask what the school can change.

An instrument loan. A marked starting point. A predictable rehearsal plan. An agreed break and a way back in. If your child wants to play trumpet, explore support for trumpet before assigning them a completely different activity.
3. Make the arrangement specific.

Who helps? Where do they go? When is it available? What happens if the room is locked or the usual adult is away? Write it down. A support nobody can find is doing a fairly poor impression of support.
For a new music program...

Ask leadership about a qualified educator, teaching time, space, equipment and costs. A club can be a beginning. Check who can attend, especially if lunch is recovery time or transport rules out staying late.
prompt: What would need to be in place for my child, and other students with similar barriers, to take part?

title: “What Could We Try Over Six Weeks?”
deck: A flexible starting plan for a school support or music opportunity. Pick a review date, not an independence deadline.
sections: Before you start: make it usable.
Agree on what you are trying, why the student wants it, who provides help and what happens if the first plan is unavailable. Choose a realistic time. There is no magic number of minutes.
Weeks 1-2: listen, show and try.
Ask about interests and barriers. Show the student where resources live and how to get help. Offer a small, workable first experience. Change anything that adds unnecessary pressure.
Weeks 3-4: keep what helps.
Build on a chosen activity or useful routine. Keep adult support available. In music, make room for actual teaching and progress on something the student wants to learn.
Weeks 5-6: ask what changed.

Can they take part and get what they need? What do they enjoy? What leaves them exhausted? Ask the student and family, then agree what continues, changes or stops. Six weeks passing does not mean support expires.

title: “What Do I Bring to the Meeting?”
deck: One example, one useful request and somewhere to write the agreement. No research dissertation required.
sections: Before: bring your child into the conversation.
Ask what they want adults to understand. They can write, draw, record a thought or ask you to speak for them. Bring a strength, a barrier and something that has helped.
During: ask for something concrete.
“Could spare worksheets be available without asking?” “What would help them join band?” “Who could help us explore a school music program?” Choose the question that fits your situation.
Before you leave: check the details.
What will the school provide? Who will show your child how to use it? When and where? What is the backup? Choose a review date and a way for your child to tell the team how it is going.
fields: The first change we agreed to try:
Who is responsible, and when it starts:
Review date and how my child will give feedback:

title: “How Do I Put This Into an Email?”
deck: A message to adapt when asking the school about support, music inclusion or a new program.
sections: 1. Fill in the parts that matter to you.
Choose one request. Add an example that helps the team understand it. Attach one useful handout or article if you want to. The entire internet can stay home.
2. Send it to someone who can help move it forward.
For your child’s support, start with their teacher or support coordinator. For a new music program, ask school leadership who should join the conversation. Include the music educator where relevant.
letter:
Subject: Could we talk about [support / music access / a music program]?

Hello [name],

I’d like to talk about [what my child or the students need]. At the moment, [one example of what is getting in the way].

Could we explore [specific request]? My hope is that students can [participate, get help, learn music or another goal], with the resources and adult support they need.

[My child says / we have noticed: ...]

I’ve included [one article or handout] to help explain what I mean. I’d appreciate your ideas about what we could put in place.

Could we agree on a first step, who will help and a time to check how it is working?

Thank you,
[Name]

title: “Does My Child Belong in Music?”
deck: Yes. Let’s talk about what makes participation possible, including PDA and neurodivergent learners.
sections: 1. Start with what they want to learn.
Trumpet? Singing? Making beats? Playing with a group? Music education is a chance to develop something your child cares about. It does not have to earn its place by fixing another subject.
2. Ask for access that means something.
“They can sit at the back” is not the whole plan. What part can they learn? Who will teach them? Could an adapted part, instrument loan, predictable routine or sound adjustment help them take part?
3. If music is missing, ask how it could begin.
A class, ensemble or creative music group needs teaching time, an educator, space and resources. Ask how costs, transport and support will be handled so the same children are not left outside again.
prompt: My child wants to [musical goal]. What could we put in place so they can learn and take part?
